messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Martin Keller was 62 when he came for treatment, a soft-spoken white man who had worked as a bank teller for decades and who now described himself as “not the same person anymore.” The event he returned to again and again had happened a year earlier in an ordinary setting that still felt unforgivably close to daily life. Leaving the bank after a long, tense Friday, he had been hurrying through a crowded sidewalk near the entrance, distracted and keyed up from work. As he turned abruptly, he collided hard with an older customer he knew by sight from the branch, knocking her off balance. She fell backward, struck the pavement, and sustained serious injuries. Martin remembered the sound of her head hitting the ground, the startled faces gathering around them, and the awful instant of recognizing her as someone he had greeted many times across the counter. What lodged most deeply was that he had caused it. Since then, people he recognizes from the bank, especially customers connected in his mind to that day, have carried a charge that feels out of proportion even to him.

In the weeks afterward, Martin became convinced that the accident revealed something damning about him. He had come to believe he was inadequate, that a decent and competent man would not have moved so carelessly, and that the way he had unraveled afterward proved he was, in his words, “a lousy coper.” He also spoke as if the incident had marked him permanently: not just that he had made a terrible mistake, but that he had changed for the worse. Those conclusions were stirred most sharply by encounters that might once have been routine. If a familiar customer stepped up to his window, or if he saw a relative of the injured woman in town, he would feel an immediate drop in his stomach and think, there you are, the man who hurts people. On especially stressful days at the bank, when the line lengthened and coworkers called questions across the counter, he became harsher with himself, taking his tension as proof that he was fundamentally not up to ordinary life anymore.

Those same beliefs also made the memory harder to keep in the past. When Martin thought of himself as damaged and inadequate, the accident did not come back as a settled recollection but as something jagged and morally charged. Remembering it brought the same terror he had felt on the sidewalk, along with an intense wave of guilt that seemed to confirm his worst conclusions about himself. He did not describe a single orderly replay. Instead, fragments arrived suddenly and without warning: the woman’s shoes leaving the pavement, the crack of impact, someone shouting for help. In those moments it felt to him as if his mind were producing evidence against him.

The memory, in turn, seemed to keep his body organized around danger. Nights became especially difficult. Martin said he could not fall asleep because some part of him felt he needed to stay alert, as though letting go would be irresponsible. Even in his own living room beside his wife, he found he could not fully relax, despite knowing rationally that he was safe. He scanned rooms, watched doorways, and startled himself by tracking other people’s movements. When fragments of the accident broke through, the surge of terror left him superalert and on guard for hours.

That ongoing state of watchfulness fed back into the way the accident returned. Because he was constantly keyed up, stress at work was no longer just unpleasant; it became a condition in which pieces of the event seemed more likely to burst in. A rushed afternoon at the bank, the press of customers he knew, even sitting tense in bed listening for small household sounds could be enough for a fragment of the sidewalk scene to flash up and disappear again. He had begun to dread sleep not only because he could not settle, but because the quiet gave the memory room to appear.

His vigilance also widened the range of what felt dangerous. Martin had become acutely sensitive to unexpected touch. If a customer brushed his sleeve while handing over a deposit slip, or a coworker touched his shoulder from behind, he reacted as if jolted, instantly bracing and scanning the room. The more on guard he stayed, the more easily ordinary stress and contact registered as threats, and familiar people at work came to feel loaded before they had even spoken. In this way his own alertness seemed to prepare the ground for the next trigger.

By the time he sought help, his world had narrowed around the branch, his home, and the effort to keep himself composed in both places. His wife had noticed that he sat rigid in the evenings and no longer tolerated even casual touch unless he saw it coming. At work he was still showing up, but familiar customers now filled him with dread because they pulled him back into the conviction that he was a man who had done irreversible harm and had never recovered properly from it. He finally came in after a stressful day at the bank when a known customer approached his window, a coworker touched him unexpectedly from behind, and he felt the memory break over him in terrified fragments. What frightened him most was not only that this could keep happening, but that it meant his view of himself was true—that he had permanently become someone weak, unsafe, and beyond repair.
